URGENCY OF NEGOTIATING AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canada has some 40 billion to 50 billion barrels of heavy oil amenable to in situ recovery. The Cold Lake heavy oil plant is the first commercial heavy oil plant, so what is at stake is not only oil supply but also commercialization of new technology which is vital to Canada's future oil self-sufficiency. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko):
That this House recognize the collapse of this project as a national emergency and request that the Prime Minister immediately involve himself directly and fully in negotiating an energy agreement with Alberta.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABANDONMENT OF PASSENGER SERVICES ON VANCOUVER ISLAND-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in light of the fact that VIA Rail has notified the government of its intention to abandon a number of passenger services, in particular the Esquimalt and Nanaimo railway service running from Victoria to Courtenay, British Columbia; in light of the order by the Canadian Transport Commission to keep that passenger service running; in view of the historic commitment inherited by VIA Rail to provide passenger service up the east coast of the island, and in light, finally, of the difficulty once a rapid transit route or system is abandoned to get it started up again, and the future needs in the area for such a system, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon);
That the government reject the application of VIA Rail to eliminate its passenger service on the E & N and require it to refrain from further announcements of this sort unless or until further public hearings are called.

subsubtopic: SUPPORT URGED FOR PASSENGER SERVICES-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise to propose a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. While most of the industrialized countries in the world are making massive investments in modernizing and expanding their rail passenger service, the Government of Canada wants to reduce passenger routes in Canada drastically. It forces VIA Rail to operate as CP and CN did, that is, if a passenger train is run old enough, late enough, slow enough, and dirty enough, nobody will get on it and the route can be abandoned. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) lays a bum rap on VIA Rail, complaining about the subsidy to VIA, and conveniently forgets to mention that all other modes of transportation receive billions of dollars in direct and indirect subsidies from the public purse. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):
That this House calls upon the government to (1) retain all present passenger routes; (2) provide VIA Rail with additional funds to invest in more new equipment, such as, at least ten more new train sets and expanded passenger routes; and, (3) provide full policy support to VIA Rail so that in a few years it can succeed so well that the taxpayers investment will be more than repaid.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the provincial governments that now employ the Royal Canadian Mounted Police under contract have been forced to consider other methods of providing police services because of the onerous and unreasonable financial demands of the federal government. That this House direct the government to moderate its financial demands and Finalize the contracts for RCMP services on the sensible cost sharing basis proposed by the provincial governments.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity I rise under the terms of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that numerous bills have been introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives that would restrict Canadian investments in the United States in retaliation for Ottawa's National Energy Program, and in view of the fact that Canadian ownership of U.S. industry is nowhere near the level of U.S. ownership in Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne):
That this House take the appropriate steps and advise the U.S. House of Representatives that such restrictive and protectionist moves would be counterproductive to the good will that Canadians and Americans have maintained over the years.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ABANDON HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister in the absence of the Prime Minister. Yesterday the Prime Minister met with seven leaders of the labour world from the seven countries which are to attend the Summit meeting here in Ottawa next week. The Prime Minister is reported to have agreed to raise their concern about the monetarism of some of the countries in the world and high interest rates, at the Summit. If that is the case, can the Deputy Prime Minister tell us if it is the intention of the government, in order to show some leadership to abandon its own high interest rate policy before the Summit? Is the government considering abandoning its high
interest rate policy to show some leadership on the world level before the Summit?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ABANDON HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICY

PRIME MINISTER'S DISCUSSIONS WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext: It is obvious that the government's policy is not working. According to an official spokesman of the President of the United States, when our Prime Minister visited that country a few days ago he did not even raise the question of high interest rates with the American President. I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister why the Prime Minister did not raise that important issue with the President of the United States, since the United States plays an important role in the world economic situation.

I have no doubt that the hon. member is interested that the question of economic policy followed in the industrialized countries will be raised at the Summit. Obviously one of the major items on the agenda is the question of general economic policy, which will be discussed. I would be very surprised if interest rates are not a subject at the forefront of the discussions. How it will be discussed is another question.

Madam Speaker, can the Deputy Prime Minister tell the House whether or not his government supports the proposition put forward by the French President, Fran$ois Mitterrand, and Chancellor Schmidt of West Germany which, in effect, is a call for economic expansion and full employment? If our government supports that policy then what action is it planning to take?

All the industrialized countries were able to agree on a communique dealing with the economy in which appropriate attention was placed on the fight against inflation and the necessity of succeeding in that fight before it would be possible to resume upward growth in the industrialized economies. 1 have no doubt that every leader at the Summit will be concerned about future growth and

It relates to the principle of ministerial responsibility and accountability. The minister will have had an opportunity to refresh his memory with respect to this whole matter. Therefore, stonewalling is not permitted. However, the minister will know the principle of which I speak, that is, the minister is responsible for everything that happens within his department, and the Prime Minister is responsible for everything that happens with respect to his ministry.
In view of the fact that the Prime Minister has admitted knowing that the cartel had an impact on Canadian prices in 1975, will the minister tell the House with which of his ministers the Prime Minister discussed this matter, and what

speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 have already indicated that we have referred the whole uranium file to the court when we decided to prosecute the six companies. That case is now before the courts. Therefore I have nothing to add about ministerial responsibility. That, of course, does not fall under my jurisdiction.

Madam Speaker, the scattered applause is quite understandable. We are not talking about the charges. We are talking about ministerial responsibility. I hope the minister understands that. A review of the annual reports of Uranium Canada, from 1970 to 1978, has indicated two interesting points. One is that Uranium Canada is a shell of a company. It has no staff. The administration and operation of Uranium Canada take place by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. The second point is that up until 1975 the president of Uranium Canada was one Jacob Austin, the deputy minister of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Shame, shame!

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR QUARTERLY INDEXATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The minister will know, I am sure, that the high, inflationary, double digit rates which we are presently experiencing impact most heavily on pensioners and other low income groups. The minister will also know that recently the Economic Council of Canada said that in spite of this government's attempts we will have double digit inflation for several years. The minister may not know, however, the fact that the Canada-Quebec Pension Plan is indexed only yearly, and that it costs Canadian pensioners under that plan some $200 a year. Does the government intend to bring in legislation to index the Canada-Quebec Pension Plan quarterly, as is done in OAS and GIS, and if so, when?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR QUARTERLY INDEXATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Canada Pension Plan will necessarily be included in the review of pension plans which we have undertaken and will continue next fall. I am very glad to know the position of the Progressive Conservative Party. This is one of its first positive recommendations concerning the pension plan review, and this aspect of the question will certainly be included in this review.

Madam Speaker, I am rather surprised that the minister shows a lack of haste on this issue. Certainly the government is now spending some $70 million on propaganda, and is spending some $268 million to subsidize the American car driver. I know that if the minister inquires from some of her officials she will find that it would only cost $70 million to bring in quarterly indexing. I would think that the minister would show greater concern.
My supplementary question concerns the fact that last spring we had a pension conference. At that time I think the Prime Minister, and also the Minister of Finance, indicated that in July there would be a pensions conference with the provinces. 1 wonder whether a date has been set for that conference and whether the terms of reference have been decided upon.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member should know that it is quite difficult for a federal minister to move on the Canada Pension Plan in, I think the word he used was a "hasty", way. It means fast. He may want to discuss this with the B.C. minister of finance or he may want to call Mr. Frank Miller of Ontario, or different ministers of finance. They do not like any changes to the Canada Pension Plan when it takes money away from them and out of the $18 billion fund that they enjoy now at preferred interest rates. That is what it does. No change can be made that rapidly by one government alone.
And the July conference? Or was that just another lie?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Trade. In light of the minister's interest in expanding overseas trade, particularly in the Orient, is he prepared to recommend to his colleagues in cabinet that Canada must abide by the international agreements that require 40 per cent of Canadian exports to be transported in Canadian registered vessels?

subsubtopic: USE OF CANADIAN REGISTERED VESSELS TO SHIP EXPORTS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I just returned from a trip to Japan and Korea where, along with businessmen from the coal industry in British Columbia, we were able to negotiate substantial contracts. Discussions have been since undertaken with the Minister of Transport and with the shipping industry, concerning this issue.

subsubtopic: USE OF CANADIAN REGISTERED VESSELS TO SHIP EXPORTS

subtopic: STEPS TO ENCOURAGE BUILDING OF CANADIAN SHIPS
STEPS TO ENCOURAGE BUILDING OF CANADIAN SHIPS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce because of his interest in industrial strategies that will create jobs. Legislation is now before the U.S. Congress which will protect the U.S. fleet at the expense of Canadian shipping. While other major trading nations are expanding their fleets and protecting their own interests, Canada continues to give away jobs by relying on foreign registered ships. As part of his so-called industrial strategy, what steps is the minister taking to ensure that we will build Canadian ships that will be registered in Canada, that will be manned by Canadian crews, and that will train a
July 15, 1981

lot of our young people for jobs that are very important to them?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STEPS TO ENCOURAGE BUILDING OF CANADIAN SHIPS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I understand that a memorandum has been tabled with the U.S. Congress suggesting that if this legislation is adopted it will increase the cost of shipping for American companies. They may well want to think twice about this proposal. In any event, Madam Speaker, at present we have underway a consultative process with the Canadian shipbuilding and ship industry, including the labour unions to develop the elements of a new national policy on shipbuilding for Canada. I hope that we will have these proposals before cabinet and ready for decision by the early fall so that Canadian companies and Canadian workers can play a major role in the very important industrial spin-offs which will come from the offshore development and the over-all development of the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: SHIPMENT OF DANGEROUS GOODS THROUGH CANADIAN PORTS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Is he aware of the fact that large quantities of radioactive materials, many of them hazardous, are presently being shipped to and from the Port of Montreal and other Canadian ports almost daily, and that these shipments are often stored for extended periods and trucked through city streets? Assuming he is aware of these practices, will the minister outline for this House the precautions which are being taken to protect shore workers, vessel crews, and citizens, from the dangers posed by these materials, and will he further undertake to provide this House with a complete inventory of all such shipments in and out of the ports of Saint John, New Brunswick; Halifax, Montreal and Vancouver during the past 18 months?

subsubtopic: SHIPMENT OF DANGEROUS GOODS THROUGH CANADIAN PORTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am surprised to see that the hon. member has not realized yet that the transportation of dangerous goods is a current event which happens every day in the whole of the Canadian economy. It is something that is desirable in terms of the economic development of Canada. There is no way one should prevent that from taking place, because one would have to stop a whole segment of the Canadian economy. Consequently the only thing governments can do in general is to take the necessary measures to make it as safe a procedure as possible. This is what takes place now.
Members were kind enough, clever enough, and wise enough to pass Bill C-18 last year, which covers exactly the transportation of dangerous goods. This is the law of the land now. I admit that the procedures and regulations are not completed,
July 15, 1981

but they are being drafted. In the meantime we are doing with the legislation we have. To give the hon. member a list of all the dangerous goods being transported in Canada at this time would probably fill his room. If that is what he wants I may try to accommodate him, but I do not think it would be very useful to him.

Madam Speaker, I have such a list there in respect of the Port of Montreal, which does not fill a room. The minister has not answered either of my questions regarding specific safeguards or specific shipments. Surely the minister must know that port workers in Montreal and elsewhere are often called upon to handle dangerous materials such as uranium hexafluoride gas, large containers of uranium concentrates and spent nuclear fuels, often without knowledge of the contents, concentrations or radiation levels, or adequate training in precautionary measures. Does he condone such laxity, and how does he justify the fact that these major ports under his jurisdiction do not even have any equipment on hand or trained personnel in place to monitor radioactivity or detect leaks?
Madam Speaker, I did not try to give the impression that we were on top of all of these questions in Canada.
You didn't?

No, I did not try to do that, because progress has to be made and progress is being made now. I am sure the hon. member has heard of the Grange Report. That Grange Report is presently being implemented, as I reported to the House recently, and five of the recommendations are before the CTC. The member seemed to imply that I should provide him with an indication of all the dangerous goods going around in Canada at this time. If he wants them limited to the port of Montreal, indeed I will try to do that. But again the name of the game is really to take all precautionary measures. He was referring to the identification of the dangerous goods themselves. Part of the Grange report recommends changes and improvements in the placarding and identification of dangerous goods, and this is going to take place.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Last week, perhaps in an attempt to rescue the uranium industry in Canada, the minister announced his intention to abandon Canada's long established nuclear safeguard policy, which includes case by case review of exported uranium for reprocessing or enrichment, and that he expects to sign a new pact with the European Economic Community in the fall.

subtopic: CANADIAN NUCLEAR SAFEGUARD POLICY-AGREEMENTS WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am afraid the hon. member has it all wrong. There are no agreements being contemplated which in any way at all weaken our commitment to nuclear nonproliferation. speechtext: There is no "Treaty Trust Fund" as such held by the government. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, sometimes when one puts a 30-second speech on the record, one is tempted to let it stand. But today I would like to speak about a bill which I consider to be one of the most important of all the bills we have dealt with in this session. In fact, in my opinon it is the most important, other than the constitutional bill.
Bill C-48 has an effect upon the country beyond just energy. This is why we are debating the amendment which was put forward so eloquently by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). It will replace the jurisdiction of the federal government over the offshore without consultation or the consent of the province.
I see the chairman of the energy committee is present this afternoon. He will know that many of us were of the understanding that this bill would not be debated until this autumn. The members of the committee received hundreds of letters from citizens across the nation who were opposed to certain sections of the bill. We attempted to deal with those letters and those concerns, as well as the concerns of hon. members of the House, by way of amendments in committee. It is rather typical of this procedure that the only amendments which were accepted were the government ones; all other ones were rejected. Hence, it was incumbent upon hon. members of the opposition who had these concerns at heart and agreed with many of them to correspond with these concerned Canadians. This is what I attempted to do in discharging my responsibilities to some 200 or 300 people and groups of people. I had the misfortune of placing those letters in the mail two days before the strike.
We are now debating this bill at report stage. The citizens have not had an opportunity to see the amendments to this bill, yet we are now being asked to rush this piece of legislation through at this time of the year. I suppose the government feels that there will not be time for native people, the many serious groups in this nation who are concerned about the effects of this bill on energy and energy production, as well as the citizens of the maritime provinces and the northern regions, to correspond with hon. members on both sides of the House respecting their concerns and the amendments they think should be put in place.
Also the chairman of the committee will recall that there was a consensus among hon. members one day. It was placed on the record by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) rather deviously, because he did it on a point of order which should have been ruled out of order. At any rate, it was placed on the record. We did not say anything about it because we felt it was an important motion. The committee members agreed unanimously that we should travel.

Yes, they did. I was present. No one objected. It was the next day that the objection came forward. This would have been important because although many witnesses came forward and gave us information as to why we should change or accept the bill, many of the members who
were on the committee did not come from those regions. It was important for members to actually spend some time in those provinces and in those areas of Canada which will be deeply affected by the bill. Of course we were not given that opportunity, and I think it is tragic in that we are now pushing the amendments through at a time when many people in the nation have not had an opportunity to get in touch with their members by mail.
Given the statement of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), the amendment of the hon. member for St. John's East has the sympathy of hon. members from the prairie provinces. We must remember that while we are dealing with this in 1981, my ancestors and those of many hon. members who sit in the House went through this very same debate from 1905 to 1930. I want to show that there is consistency between what happened then and what is happening now. It is the very same type of argument.
First I should like to read from the speech of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, as reported on page 11472 of Hansard, wherein he stated:
They believe this should be up to the provinces, territorial governments or other groups. That is not our view. Our view is that those lands belong to all the people of Canada. The immense wealth that is there belongs to the people of Canada as a whole.
The Parliament of Canada is the guardian and trustee of the immense wealth which should be developed and protected in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole and the people of the regions concerned in particular. That is our view.
Basically that comes down to the feeling of many of my constituents, that feeling of alienation, of not being in total control of their resources. This feeling is still in place today. If anyone believes that it is in any way waning, that is not the case. It is grinding them further into the ground. They are placing their feet down firmer than ever. I do not want to be a member of this House in a few years, hearing the same thing coming from my friends from Nova Scotia and Newfoundland or, hopefully, soon, from the provinces of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
Because of my own interest and because of the feelings of my constituents and my family over the years, I went back in the debates to see what happened then. I found that what happened then is very consistent with what is happening now. The Hon. R. B. Bennett speaking on April 29, 1930, summarized the argument very well. The Liberal Party of that time believed that the ownership of the resources of the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta should continue to be, for the good of Canada under the jurisdiction of Canada, and that other provinces which came into Confederation earlier would have their resources under their own control.
I would like to quote briefly from the Hon. R. B. Bennett's speech. He said:
Twenty-five years ago this fall, in the House of Commons, the Liberal party unequivocally placed itself on record as being opposed to the granting of these resources to the western provinces. On a division, which is recorded in Hansard, the Liberal party of that day decided that the new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan should not possess their resources. The Conservative party of that
July 15, 1981

day believed that they would not be provinces, within the meaning of that word, under the constitution, if they were deprived of their resources; they believed that the administration of the public domain within the area of Alberta and Saskatchewan by the Crown in right of the Dominion was at variance with every principle that should govern the creation of new provinces, and they placed themselves on record accordingly.
There are other interesting situations raised in the speech of the Hon. R. B. Bennett. He indicated that the Conservative governments of Borden and Meighen committed themselves to turning the resources over to the provinces. However, they were unable to do so. First, they were not given the chance to do so because of the war. They had to deal with very important matters and were not able to get the bill on. The second reason was the very short period of time that that party was in government. The Conservative party kept true to its commitment. When it came into power within a few months of the speech from which I have quoted, Mr. Bennett transferred the ownership of the resources to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Today we are debating the same question. It is whether the resources under the ocean, off the shores of those provinces, or found on islands a few miles off the shores of those provinces, should be under the control of the provinces. We know what the argument is on the other side. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has had a great deal of trouble with pesky provinces. He does not like to lower himself to work out an agreement. He wants control. He wants the power. Thus, we see the energy agreement which should have been worked out months ago with Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia not being worked out, although rigs are being driven from the area and tar sands and heavy oil plants which should be going ahead are not going ahead.
In my opinion there is a plan to all this. The plan is to move that capital into the offshore and into the north. The government is really not that concerned about getting new energy sources from Alberta or the prairie provinces as long as it can see its way free, hopefully, to getting those resources from the offshore or the north. But far be it for the government to allow pesky provinces to get in the road.
I can outline for the minister and the country my feelings on how the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has been systematically dismantled. In effect, Alberta is a province, and the minister of energy does not want the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) in his way when he permits land to be explored by Petro-Canada and other companies. Nor does he want to concern himself with the provinces of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia when development and drilling is given the go-ahead in that part of the country. The whole question is one of control of development and control of money. Is the federal government poorer because Alberta is richer? Are the provinces of Ontario, B.C., or Quebec poorer because Alberta is richer? Many on the opposite side of the House tend to think so. They tend to think that somehow it is wrong for a province which has legitimate control of its resources to spend the wealth from those resources in the interests of Canadians. They say that is not right. They think that it is far better for
Canada Oil and Gas Act
the nation to have control of the resources and of the wealth and to see that it is spent in the national interest. As my colleague has said many times, that wealth is squandered, which is why the provinces fight so hard to maintain control of their resource wealth. In many cases they have shown the ability to better spend it in the national interest.
It was stated by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) that the average income of the citizens of Newfoundland is in the area of $4,000. That is probably one of the lowest average incomes in the nation. In the same manner as we in Alberta and Saskatchewan saw the ability to fully participate in this nation through the wealth of our resources, so do the people of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia see the ability to participate in this country as full participants. They see the chance to create work and wealth in their own area rather than to live without the knowledge that their jobs will always be there or, in many cases, without the knowledge that they will be perpetually on unemployment insurance or welfare. They now see an opportunity.
When we look at the bill which is before us, we see the federal government attempting to grab that opportunity. The government is saying, "Well, we will allow you to have the wealth of that resource until your average income is the same as that of other provinces. Then you must come to us again for handouts because we will want control of the resources again." We in this party do not feel that is acceptable. Our feelings have been consistent on this question.
When the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) was prime minister, he met with the Premier of the province of Nova Scotia. The correspondence which was transmitted between the two parties is available to all members. The then prime minister laid out the feelings of this party with regard to offshore control and ownership of mineral resources. I would like to read from a letter dated August 23, 1979. The then prime minister said:
It is our belief that this challenge can only be met if the province has ownership of and jurisdiction over its offshore mineral resources. Accordingly, we greatly appreciate your support of Newfoundland's position and the position of the federal Conservative party that Newfoundland's undersea resources should be treated constitutionally in the same manner as if they were on land.
It is almost the same as saying that the oil which is under Wizard Lake in Alberta is not owned by the province of Alberta.

It is almost the same as saying that because there is a few feet of water over what is legitimately the land mass in Newfoundland, it is no longer possible for it to be under the jurisdiction or the control of that province. I want to show what I believe is happening as it is a major area, as is confirmed by what is happening under the National Energy Program and under this bill. By driving the rigs out of Alberta, we are losing an opportunity of finding billions of barrels of oil and natural gas. This government believes, and I hope it is right, that it can bring on stream from Hibernia and

offshore Nova Scotia, and in the north, substantially more oil than could come from drilling in Alberta, even from the building of those tar sands plants and heavy oil plants. 1 believe that to be a risk that we should not be taking in Canada. While we should continue very strongly in the exploration of these two regions, we should not do it to the detriment of what we know to be possible in the western deposits of Alberta, Saskatchewan and B.C.
A forecast by a technical paper provided by this federal government suggests that 22,000 exploration wells must be drilled in western Canada in the next 10 years to find some 2.6 billion barrels of oil. It states that, by comparison, only 75 wells drilled in the Mackenzie Valley could discover the same amount of oil. The same is true for even less drilling in Hibernia. That may be so, and I hope it is true; but it is because of this policy that we are perhaps losing-and many say we are losing-energy self-sufficiency because we may not be able to bring that resource on in time.
However, in conclusion, I have to say that my argument today-and I will have a chance to make other arguments because there are many amendments to this bill-is that we in the western part of this nation have a great deal of sympathy for this amendment and support it wholehearedly because we believe that the people of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland are fighting the same battle that our ancestors fought from 1905 to 1930 when they were finally given jurisdiction over those resources. In my opinion, there should be no argument, politically or morally, about this question, even though the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) may say that there is some argument legally. What I am afraid is that we will be facing-

speechtext: -the same kind of alienation in those areas that we are now facing in Alberta. It disturbs me a great deal that citizens of that area are questioning their citizenship.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the amendment to Bill C-48 which we are debating today is designed, according to the mover, to prevent Bill C-48 from imposing federal ownership and control upon the offshore areas of Canada. The arguments we have heard from the opposition during the last three days have repeated this assumption, which is totally incorrect. Bill C-48 simply does not do that. The bill does not, in any way, alter the relationship between the federal and provincial governments with regard to offshore ownership and control.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Why did you put them in there, then?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
That question is a matter for decision by the courts. All Bill C-48 does is to provide rules to regulate oil and gas interests in Canada lands. According to Bill C-48:
"Canada lands" means lands that belong to Her Majesty in right of Canada, or in respect to which Her Majesty in right of Canada has the right to dispose of or exploit the natural resources-
Bill C-48 does not declare the offshore areas to be Canada lands. That is a legal question. If there are areas offshore
which the courts declare not to be Canada lands, then Bill C-48 does not apply to them.
I would not go so far as to label the amendment specious, because it at least allows us in this House to debate the fundamental issues regarding ownership and control of our offshore. However, I would argue that the amendment before us is certainly unnecessary because Bill C-48 does not do what the amendment pretends to do and pretends to correct. It is not necessary to correct something which is not there. However, the basic issues involved here are important, and they do reflect a very fundamental difference between the positions of the two major parties in this House.
The government, I hope-and I believe it does-starts with the premise that the resources of both our northern territories and our offshore areas are the common heritage of all Canadians and are the basis for a common sharing, the vision of which can help to bind Canada together. Canadians, whether living in Alberta, British Columbia, or Quebec, are part owners of the resources of the Yukon, the Northwest Territories, or offshore of those two territories. Surely, that form of joint ownership, that heritage we share together, does mean something to people. I am practical enough to think that people are a little selfish, and that no matter what province they live in, if they feel there is something there of which we all have a part, it is part of the cement, or can be part of the cement, that binds this country together. It is all very well to talk in flowery terms about sentiment binding this country together. I think there has to be more than sentiment. As a matter of fact, we all know that there is a lot more than sentiment binding the country together. There are a lot of practical things, and this is one of them.
When I say that, I want to preface that statement with a commitment which, I presume, has been made by the present Government of Canada and has been made in the past by Liberal governments, that Canadians living in those areas of the north or in the maritime regions, should have first call on those offshore or northern resources to assure themselves of a standard of living which is second to none in Canada. We are using different terminology here, but the former minister of northern affairs from Manitoba, who spoke two days ago in the House, came very close to using almost the same wording. Although I was quite pleased to hear him say it the other day, he did not say it when he was minister of northern affairs; namely, that what we want, first of all, is that the people of the north have a first call on their resources. He did not use those precise terms, but we all agree that those people should have the first chance to benefit. The people of the maritimes and people in Newfoundland should certainly have the first call on the resources which lie off their shores. And so much the better, Mr. Speaker.
If the reserves are larger than is predicted, I doubt if many Newfoundlanders would object to sharing the additional icing on the cake with Canadians across the continent. The same is true with regard to maritimes living in Nova Scotia. When it comes to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, the amendment does not make it clear whether it deliberately left out any reference to the offshore resources. The former Conservative government under its prime minister, promised to create a province in the Yukon, which, by example, would have required the creation of one or more provinces in the Northwest Territories.
This promise of provincehood, combined with the position of the former prime minister on offshore resources, would have meant that those new provinces would have requested not only that the land based resources be turned over to them but also the resources offshore. The total population of the Yukon is about 25,000 and of the Northwest Territories about 55,000; together they make up about .3 per cent of the Canadian population. When Manitoba entered confederation with a population of 12,000 to 15,000, its percentage of the Canadian total was about .6 per cent or .7 per cent. The population of the two northern territories only comes to about .3 per cent of the Canadian population today. When Prince Edward Island entered confederation, its population represented about 1.2 per cent of the Canadian total. This undercuts some of the arguments being advanced for provincehood.
While some elected officials in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon are pushing for provincehood immediately, very few people on the streets support the idea. I do not believe that the majority of people in the territories regard provincehood as a reasonable, near-term objective.
The potential for problems accompanying provincehood is substantial. A very small group of people could control the immense resources which our government maintains are the common heritage of all Canadians. I cannot imagine reasonable people anywhere in Canada believing that it is wise to create provinces in the north and to promise to turn over these immense resources to them.
What northerners need is a way to cut through red tape. Some members of the House are inclined to paint a picture of poor northern colonials, but in fact the small population in the north has more absolute control over its own destiny than any other group in the country. For example, 25,000 people in the Yukon control their own education system. What other group
Canada Oil and Gas Act
of 25,000 or 100,000 people in the country control their education? Northerners are not colonized, as many people in this House, particularly on the other side, would maintain. They are in control of their own lives.
That is not to say, Mr. Speaker, that there are not areas of frustration that could not be improved or that the federal government could not find mechanisms to enable people in the north to solve their problems in a more direct way. Improvements are possible.
I feel that we should not be looking at provincehood as the only possible long-term goal for government of those two northern territories, but that we should be looking for another form of government which would give the people of the north control over their destinies and, at the same time, give them more direct, effective, efficient democracy and self-government. Provincehood is not necessarily the right thing for them. In fact, what we do in the north might show all Canadians that a new form of government is possible; one that allows all of us to be governed in a more effective and efficient manner.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand it, the specific matter now before the House is motion No. 3 which amends the definition section of clause 2 of Bill C-48. Clause 2 of Bill C-48 contains a definition that establishes the territory included in the term "Canada lands", and that is what the pith and substance of motion No. 3 is, to change that definition of "Canada lands" to exclude those lands which lie off the coast of Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and which in the bill are referred to as the submarine land.
I have had an opportunity on two previous occasions when Bill C-48 which enacts the Canada Oil and Gas Act was before the House on second reading; on December 17, 1980, and again on January 12, 1981, to outline the history of the province of Nova Scotia's claim to its offshore resources contained in the submarine lands that adjoin the coast of Nova Scotia. I will not repeat them on this occasion.
1 will underline the fact that for centuries now the province of Nova Scotia has claimed these resources and the submarine lands. The government of Canada, on the other hand, prior to 1968 or thereabouts, made no claim to these same submarine lands and at no time purported to deal with the natural resources that may be buried in these lands.
The history of the matter in that connection stems from a Supreme Court of Canada decision in 1968 when the resources that were contained in the submarine lands off the coast of British Columbia were considered by the Supreme Court of Canada. In what became known as the reference respecting British Columbia Resources, the Supreme Court in its wisdom to belong to Canada and not the province of British Columbia and, consequently, the resources within them. That decision of the Supreme Court was by no means complete in that it purported to extend to all submarine lands adjoining the coast of Canada, whether on the Pacific or the Atlantic coasts. Nor was it complete with respect to submarine lands adjoining the coast of British Columbia. In fact, I read a very recent report that the government of British Columbia wants to bring again before the court the matter of ownership of specific areas adjoining the coast of British Columbia on the basis that those particular areas were not covered by the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada which was made in 1968.
Even with respect to the specifics of that decision, and with regard to the claims of the government of the province of British Columbia to its own coastline, the decision of the
Supreme Court of Canada cannot be taken as complete and undisputed.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, you will readily understand how the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada which relates to British Columbia lands is not accepted by either the government of Newfoundland or the government of Nova Scotia as resolving the dispute regarding the lands adjacent to their coast.
Let me speak very briefly about the history of the particular provisions we now have before us incorporated in Bill C-48 and which will become part of the Canada Oil and Gas Act if this bill is enacted.
The Parliament of Canada, following the decision regarding B.C. resources in 1968, enacted a new provision to the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act. This particular provision applied all provisions in that act to the submarine lands off the coast of Canada, but it did not in that provision claim those lands for Canada. It simply said the provisions of that act, the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, would apply to those lands, which is quite different, I believe, from the provisions we now have before us as part of the definition section of clause 2 of Bill C-48.
I want to be very specific about that because I disagree completely with the remarks of the hon. member for Chateau-guay (Mr. Watson), which were very similar to the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren), the member for Etobicoke North, in this House the other day on this same subject matter.
The thrust of their remarks, as I understood them, was that the definition of Canada lands now contained in Bill C-48 does not in itself claim or expropriate the submarine lands off the coast of Nova Scotia, or the coast of Newfoundland for the federal authority. It simply applies the provisions of Bill C-48 to those lands by way of describing them in the term "Canada lands".
I reject that interpretation of clause 2 of the bill defining Canada lands in light of the other provisions of the bill, because in fact the bill defines Canada lands very clearly to include areas like Sable Island and submarine lands up to the 200-mile limit off the coast of Canada. Also in another clause of the bill it claims and provides that the act applies to those very Canada lands.
That is simply not the technique that would be used if the purpose of the very careful definition of Canada lands was simply to allow the federal legislation to apply to those lands. We all know, who have studied these matters, that the federal authority has the simple right and authority to legislate in respect of many matters including natural resources, in some of their respects. Certainly the federal authority has the right and authority under the British North America Act to legislate with regard to environmental matters on the coast, whether or not they affect provincial resources.
July IS, 1981

In addition, by a clause of the bill, the provisions of the act are binding on Her Majesty in right of Canada or a province. That provision is contained in clause 5(4) of the bill. There is a clear intention evidenced in the bill, through the definition section and through the fact that clause 5(1) makes all the provisions applicable to Canada lands, and because of the fact that the bill by clause 5(4) is binding on Her Majesty the Queen in right of a province. There is, I believe, a clear claim to what is described as Canada lands, and it just simply cannot be put aside on the basis that if any court subsequently decides that the province of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia or any other provinces own submarine lands adjacent to their coast, then the act will not operate in that area. That is not true, and I think the provinces, particularly the province of Nova Scotia, see Bill C-48 as a claim to the submarine lands which have been historically claimed by the province of Nova Scotia.
Just to demonstrate that there is a clear conflict, I remind the House that the province of Nova Scotia, in the case of its petroleum resources act enacted in 1980, claims the very lands which are covered by the definition of Canada lands in Bill C-48. We have a conflict on the face of the two pieces of legislation, the Nova Scotia petroleum resources act and the proposed Canada Oil and Gas Act. Both purport to deal with exactly the same lands. If that is not a conflict and if that is not a claim by the respective jurisdictions, on the one hand the province of Nova Scotia and on the other hand the Government of Canada, I do not know what is. We ought not to be lulled into thinking that there is no problem here and that we can go ahead and not deal with the conflict in this House and allow some other authority to deal with it, because that would be to abandon our responsibilities and not to face up to the problem which exists.
Let me very briefly review the claim of the province of Nova Scotia which, as I have said, I have detailed on other occasions in this House. Basically, the province of Nova Scotia was established by a grant by King James I which gave to Sir William Alexander, in 1621, a band of land extending seaward for 120 miles, and it included Sable Island. Subsequent treaties confirmed these boundaries for the province of Nova Scotia. And, in 1867, when the British North America Act was enacted, Section 7 of that Act said that the province of Nova Scotia consists of the land, mines and minerals which belonged to that province at the time of confederation. The basis for Nova Scotia's claim is very clear. I will not purport to deal with the claim of the province of Newfoundland.
What do we do, given this claim by the province of Nova Scotia and the historic basis for the claim and given the existence of these two pieces of legislation, provincial on the one hand and federal on the other hand, claiming exactly the same land, the submarine lands off the coast of Nova Scotia? What do we do? We have a dispute, and we must resolve it.
How can the dispute be resolved? One way would be for the province of Nova Scotia or any other province interested in resolving the dispute simply to sit down with the Government of Canada in a sensible, practical way to work out the prob-
Canada Oil and Gas Act
lem. But we all know that that is not the style and the method employed by the Government of Canada, not only in this area of natural resources but also in the constitutional area and in any other area, including medicare and any other problem which comes up. It is simply not the way, method and style of the Government of Canada to resolve disputes by sensible political negotiation. Indeed, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) confirmed in this House that as far as he was concerned, that method had been exhausted by perhaps a few meetings, which established very little, if anything. Notwithstanding that most sensible Canadians would have the dispute resolved by negotiation, the federal authority has refused to continue these negotiations and presents us with the provisions of Bill C-48 which, as I have said, is effectively a claim of the submarine lands off the coast of Nova Scotia.
Another simple method of settling this dispute would be to extend the boundaries of the province of Nova Scotia to include those lands, in the same way that this very House of Commons extended the boundaries of various provinces, including the province of Ontario and the province of Manitoba, in 1912 and 1913. Again, the Government of Canada has refused to follow this course of action and has claimed the offshore resources and the submarine lands to the extent of 200 miles and to the continental shelf, not for the people of Canada but for the Government of Canada. There is a very substantial difference.
It has been claimed in this House on several occasions by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and by the Prime Minister that they would be willing to settle the dispute with the province of Nova Scotia and the other coastal provinces, but the manner in which they propose to settle the dispute is not one which could possibly be acceptable to the government of Nova Scotia.
What the Government of Canada proposes by way of settling the dispute is to take over the submarine lands and the resources in those lands, to dictate the manner by which those lands and the time in which those lands are developed, to exercise full and complete control over all aspects of exploration and development and then, having done that, to return to the participating provinces a percentage of the revenues. The Prime Minister has even said that this percentage could rise to 100 per cent if that would resolve the dispute but, as well all know, 100 per cent of nothing is exactly that, nothing. So without any guarantee of what those revenues are going to be, for the Government of Canada to offer to the provinces 65 per cent, 75 per cent or even 100 per cent is to say nothing. What the province of Nova Scotia wants is the ability to develop those resources and, more particularly, to assist the private sector to develop those resources and to co-operate with the oil exploration and development industry to see that the resources in the submarine lands are developed as quickly as possible.
It should not surprise anyone in this House that the province of Nova Scotia and, indeed, the people of Nova Scotia have serious doubts about the willingness and the desire of the Government of Canada to bring about the development of offshore resources in submarine lands with the rapidity and at

July 15, 1981
Canada OH and Gas Act
the quick pace necessary to allow the province of Nova Scotia to continue its economic progress.
Unfortunately, settlement of the dispute comes down again, as in the case of any dispute I have ever been involved in, to the good faith and responsibility of the parties to that dispute. And we in Nova Scotia have seen no evidence on the part of the Government of Canada that it is willing to act in good faith and in a responsible manner to resolve this dispute. The federal government offers only a share of the resources without indicating in any way what that share might be. To myself and to many Nova Scotians, this is nothing more than a continuation of the charity payments, transfer payments and aid which have been provided by the Government of Canada in the past. And it will simply ensure for the future, as in the past, the economic plight of the maritime area.
There are a number of other items which relate to the particular provisions we now have before us in relation to the development of the Canada lands. And I want to point out to all hon. members of this House that the real heart of the problem and the real effect of the dispute is that it is impeding development of the offshore resources in the submarine lands. My colleagues on the other side of the House might not be willing to accept my word for that, but I have as support the word of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan) and of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), who have both said publicly on many occasions that the dispute with respect to ownership of offshore resources was hindering the development of those resources. I do not have to detail what that means in terms of lost jobs and general losses to the economy at a point in time when Nova Scotians and, indeed, all Canadians require jobs and an impetus to our economy in order to stimulate activity and produce employment.
So in that context, Mr. Speaker, we must review the background and necessity for resolving this dispute concerning ownership and development of offshore resources. It is recognized by individual members of the government, members on this side, and people in the oil and gas industry that the dispute is impeding the development of offshore resources.
How are we going to resolve that dispute, Mr. Speaker? We are certainly not going to do it by bringing into this House legislation which vests the Nova Scotia and Newfoundland offshore resources in the Government of Canada. That will only prolong the dispute and lead to litigation. I have asked the Prime Minister in this House: "What are you going to do to resolve the dispute?" His response has been that he would be willing to have the matter go before the courts. No one agrees, Mr. Speaker, that that is the way to resolve the dispute. However, there is in fact now before the courts, as I believe the parliamentary secretary pointed out, a case involving the question of ownership of offshore resources. So, Mr. Speaker, we cannot avoid the fact that if Parliament does not take steps to resolve the dispute, someone outside this House will do so before the courts.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, in relation to the definition of Canada lands and the fact they include the offshore areas of Nova Scotia, I appeal to the government to review its position, to reconsider Nova Scotia's claim and the economic plight of the people of Nova Scotia. I appeal to the government to formulate a sensible policy to deal with this dispute, one which will result in its resolution in a sensible and fair way to the people of Nova Scotia and the people of Canada as a whole, so that we can pursue our economic interests to their benefit.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity this afternoon to join in this debate on Bill C-48 at report stage. I would say at the outset that my position as a member from Ontario is somewhat different from that of those from the extremes of our country and that my perspective, in terms of what this bill is doing and might do to the established relationships, in so far as natural resources are concerned, between the provinces and the government, is perhaps without some of the perceived vested interests which are apparent in members from either side of the country. That perspective comes from a position which has been gradually formed by watching the development of natural resources in this country, and what the federal government has done with those resources over a long period of time, particularly this Liberal government.
Before commenting on the motion, I would like to say that at a time when the country is faced with extreme problems in the economy, when we are in the middle of a mail strike which has put considerably more stress on major segments of our people, whether it is business or individuals, it seems passing strange to me that we are now using this time at the discretion of the government to deal with things which I think are important in the long term but really do nothing to resolve the economic distress we now have in Canada. I think that is an unfortunate circumstance, one which we are prepared to face, but we would really rather be doing what I think in the short term could benefit Canadians across the country.
Bill C-48, Mr. Speaker, does a number of things through the back door that deserve full attention head on, and which could have been dealt with in the years gone by in a way which would have taken away a lot of the difficulties which are apparent in the bill. We are dealing specifically with one of those areas, namely, the Canada lands. Looking at that as a separate issue, at any other time would deserve the full attention of the House in a separate bill. It comes to the core of things which go back as far as confederation, in fact one of the primary concerns of the BNA. It was an evolution of events from the time of the BNA which have put us in the spot we are in now. There is no question that in the British North America Act we have a definition of provincial control over natural resources. Section 109 states:
All lands, mines, minerals, and royalties belonging to the several provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick at the union, and all sums then due or payable for such lands, mines, minerals, or royalties, shall belong to the several provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick in
July 15, 1981

which the same are situate or arise, subject to any trusts existing in respect thereof, and to any interest other than that of the province in the same.
That having been said, obviously the question of the resources under the sea was left out. This issue, as it developed through the progression of Canada as a nation, through the Treaty of Versailles, through the Statutes of Westminster and even up until now, has still been unresolved. It is a question faced by all countries when they look at their sovereignty, the control of their territorial waters and their international dealings.
I would like to go back one step to look at this amendment as it attempts to separate from the Canada lands the offshore areas of the provinces on the extremes of the country. The premise of the amendment to clause 2, presented now as motion No. 3, is based on the four criteria provided in the undertaking of the former Clark government and Mr. Peck-ford. Those four principles are as follows: Number one, that the province of Newfoundland should own the mineral resources of the continental margin in so far as Canada should own them; number two, that ownership and legislative jurisdiction would be consistent with and subject to the division of legislative competence as between Parliament and the provincial legislatures under the Constitution of Canada; number three, that the Government of Canada would continue to have legislative jurisdiction in certain areas such as the environment, shipping and so on; number four, those principles would be confirmed by the signing of an agreement between the two governments and by appropriate legislative action and constitutional change.
That arrangement could have provided the premise of a rational ongoing situation appropriate not only to Newfoundland, but it would also have provided a potential basis for dealing with British Columbia and the other Atlantic provinces. It could also be seen in light of developments in British Columbia and in terms of things which have already happened since the entrance into confederation of Newfoundland. It has been mentioned by the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has suggested these things could be resolved in the Supreme Court. We go back to the British Columbia situation where mineral rights were given to that province in a 1968 decision of the Supreme Court.
There is an interesting and probably important parallel to be looked at in the situation with the United States. In 1974 they had a similar situation in a case called the United States v. California, which was resolved in favour of the United States, concerning control over mineral resources. I think it should clearly establish their resolve and the parallel that could be drawn in terms of how we might resolve some of our situations in Canada.
I would like to read briefly the comment of Mr. Robert B. Krueger concerning the management of federal petroleum resources in the United States. It very clearly defines the decision which was taken in 1953 that reversed the original
Canada Oil and Gas Act
court decision of 1947. He said that the situation is that the various coastal states own the mineral resources in the three-mile territorial sea surrounding the United States. This was directly as a result of the submerged lands act of 1953. One quesiton which will quickly come to mind concerns this three-league territorial sea. "Three-league" is one of the terms of reference in a number of comments; it would actually be nine miles. We must ask whether a specific mileage is in fact at stake. Indeed it is, because the 200-mile territorial limit is considerably different than that. That is really the argument.
If the Supreme Court of the United States made a decision in that regard, I am not clear as to how far other rights extend into the territorial waters. It would seem clear to me that the definition we require at the present time is an understanding and a rationalization of what limits there will be in terms of not only the main controls of the federal government with respect to the environment and other matters which relate to the federal government and sovereignty, but also in terms of a definition of the mileage and under what terms the agreement might take place.
There is major room for discussion, but I make the point that this agreement should take place not by the back door through Bill C-48, but through a rationalization, an understanding and an agreement which is sensible to the whole country.
The prime question in so far as Bill C-48 is concerned, and many of the items which antagonize and concern the provinces, is not the one respecting the legislative direction of the government. In itself that is one question which might be handled in one manner, but the overriding concern of all hon. members on this side of the House is the competence of the federal government as exercised by the Liberal party when dealing with issues that are important to all Canadians if we are to achieve the goals of self-sufficiency, of management of the country and the economy, and of all things we need to develop the potential of the country. This would be the primary concern. It is the one which is addressed by the reaction of the provinces to the mechanism of takeover which the federal government is providing under the terms of Bill C-48.
If we look at the examples of competence of the Liberal government, the one which hits us in the face very quickly is the situation in the Post Office. There have been six strikes in the last five years, and we are in the middle of one now. What kind of competence is that? What kind of competence is there in the situation respecting VIA Rail which is withdrawing services that are important to certain areas when in fact it is supposed to be providing them. What kind of competence is there in other areas such as AECL with $800 million in excess requirements this year? What kind of competence is there in the management of any number of government departments? I could repeatedly give examples of the incompetence as expressed by the kind of management not only in those areas, but in the area of natural resources which the federal government now wants to take over.
On top of all of this, there are examples of where ministerial discretion is requested and provided in Bill C-48. Not only is a

July 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
system being put in place now, but we are also asking that the minister, at any given point in time in any number of areas described in the bill, will be given an opportunity to exercise powers in a discretionary manner which are overwhelming in terms of the eventual outcome. It would make me insecure and very uncomfortable if we gave these controls to the federal government now.
An interesting comment appeared in a newspaper article two or three days ago. Although in normal circumstances I might not be the first person to quote Sylvia Ostry, I think her comments were in support of the argument I should like to make in terms of the ability of the federal government to do what is required. In part, the article reads:
"We are the most resource-rich country in the OECD," she said, perching excitedly on the edge of the sofa in her office.
But the real question is, why isn't our performance a hell of a lot better?
"Inflation in Canada isn't decelerating and there are disquieting signs of it creeping up. Given Canada's underlying growth potential, why shouldn't we be better than anyone else?"
It is obvious who has been in charge, who has been running things, and who has been taking us where we are going.
1 should like to refer to the points which were raised by the Parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren). While there might be some question as to the relevance, I suggest that in some ways the government has put its statements forward and that the parliamentary secretary speaks for the government, so my comments are relevant. He talked directly about self-sufficiency, which was one of the key phrases of a previous government to this Liberal government. It is one of the main points in terms of the energy future of Canada. Self-sufficiency under the terms of the National Energy Program and Bill C-48, as one of the many parts of the National Energy Program, is in severe difficulty. We had reasonable chances to reach self-sufficiency by 1990 under the different approaches which could have been taken. The single goal of self-sufficiency is severely threatened now, not only by Bill C-48 but by the general attitude of the government. In support of that point, I should like to quote from an article which arose from a Woods Gordon report. It reads as follows:
In 1990 assuming demand has not grown, and using the NEP's optimistic supply forecast (which does not provide for frontier production but includes oil sands production),-
This is very debatable now.
-Canada would experience a shortfall of 330,000 barrels per day. The NEP document states "it would be premature and unwise to count on the frontier to solve the oil supply problem." A CPA forecast (which does not include frontier production or new tar sands production) results in a shortfall of 740,000 barrels per day by 1990. Under current provisions of the NEP the CPA does not believe it will be possible to develop new frontier and tar sands production and does believe that the decline in conventional oil production will be more severe than previously forecast.
This comment was made by several groups which pointed out very well that we will simply not achieve the important goal of self-sufficiency.
Also the parliamentary secretary raised the issue of revenue. In looking at these offshore resources, there is no question that
the government is looking at revenue which it says is required to maintain the services it is providing to Canadians. One of the subtle elements about all this is whether or not the government is receiving revenue or has mechanisms in place to achieve revenue through regulation, taxation systems and so on, without becoming involved in a confrontation with the provinces which causes difficulty in terms of Canadian unity and the other matters that are straining the different parts of the cohesion of the country.
As a late comment I should like to indicate how the price of a gallon of gasoline is shared at the present time in terms of revenue. In terms of dollars per barrel of gasoline, $18 goes to the federal government. Approximately $8 goes to the provincial governments, whether it be the government of Ontario through road taxes or the government of Alberta through royalties. Some $6 goes to the producer and $11 to the refiner. About $3 goes to the dealer. Thus, the lion's share still goes to the federal government in the ratio of about three times that which goes to any other part of the system.
Total increases in the cost of crude oil in 1981 alone could exceed $8 per barrel by next fall. Of this amount the producing provinces and the oil companies will share approximately $2 per barrel and the remaining $6 will go to the Liberal government. That might be justifiable if we could see that it was really going toward self-sufficiency, increased production and everything which we think is important in terms of our energy resources. The fact of the matter is we do not have anything else to show for it. What we have had so far is $8 billion having gone to Petro-Canada, which has given us approximately 3 per cent more Canadianization. Another $25 billion will have to be raised either through Petro-Canada or some other vehicle in order to bring us up to the so-called Canadianization level which the government wants. That is a massive amount of money. But what has been done to develop our resources? Precious little. This has a great deal to do with control but very little to do with the development of resources.
My final point, and the point on which I would like to end my speech, has to do with my perspective as an Ontario member. There is no explanation for the fact that we are not doing a hell of a lot better than we are, as Sylvia Ostry said. The only explanation is that the perspective we should have, if we are to develop not only our natural resources but all of our other talents in the industry, must be in terms of private enterprise. The perspective which governments should have must be one of co-operation and the understanding that it is the private sector which will develop these resources under the appropriate controls of governments, both federal and provincial. This must be done not through the confrontationist style which has been so apparent and predominant in all the dealings thus far but through the kind of thinking which will develop as a result of negotiation and settlement, which is necessary if we are to achieve our goals.
