speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this point in the debate 1 should like to comment on the amendment of our Progressive Conservative colleagues which is aimed at reducing the size of Canada lands by not including the 200-mile offshore limit. Everything considered, I must say that as a Canadian and a Quebecer 1 do not feel ashamed to think that the national government must play a leading role in the protection of Canada lands. It is that particular aspect which I would like to debate with my colleagues this afternoon. First of all, Mr. Speaker, allow me to recall the historical background of the question under study. We are examining a bill which has to do with the energy issue, petroleum and gas. The principle involved with respect to the extension of the territory to 200 miles offshore to cover such natural resources as petroleum and gas has given rise to fascinating events in Canada. Indeed it goes back several years and I consulted a publication by a famous author whose name is listed in the 1970 Canadian yearbook on international law. Mr. Jacques-Yvan Morin, currently a minister in the PQ government, wrote an interesting article on technical progress, pollution and the recent evolution of the law of the sea in Canada, particularly with respect to the Arctic. I therefore believe that he is a very neutral authority to comment on this topic. In this rather long article, 25 or 30 pages, which I have no intention of quoting at length, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to an excerpt from Mr. Jacques-Yvan Morin's article who wrote on page 158 of that publication that the extension of Canada's ownership of the offshore territory, or rather not the extension of the territory but the extension of certain rights from three to twelve miles- from twelve to 100 miles in the Canadian Arctic-was an extremely constructive measure.
On page 215, Mr. Morin mentions the legislation passed by the Canadian government and notes that everywhere else in Canada, the limit was 12 miles and that the new legislation would extend this to 100 miles offshore to protect the environment. Of course, this issue had arisen as a result of a tanker accident causing an oil spill on the Canadian coastal territory, and the limit was finally extended thanks to the dynamic action of the Canadian government. Indeed, in 1972, with Bills 201 and 202, the Liberal government of the time extended the limits of three miles, 12 miles and 100 miles unilaterally to 200 miles. However, this action was accompanied by international discussions to determine who owned the offshore resources of Canada.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, Canada is bordered by three oceans, the Arctic, the Atlantic and the Pacific, and by extending the territory of Canada beyond the 12-mile limit, Canada would be able to increase the potential of its natural resources by about 20 per cent. The knowledge that Canada will be able to develop these resources in the future has an interesting impact in terms of the gross national product. The
Canada Oil and Gas Act
international discussions to ratify the treaty implementing the 200-mile limit without the threat of international disputes are under way, and 1 am confident that every country with coastal territories rich in natural resources will certainly support this extremely desirable action, especially because when we speak about coastal territories, we are obviously speaking about resources, but also about the development of these resources.
By excluding the submarine areas located outside of a province, adjacent to the coast of Canada and extending throughout the natural extension of the land territory of Canada to the outer edge of the continental shelf or to a distance of 200 nautical miles from the baselines, Bill C-48 is extremely positive and will only reinforce the very dynamic action undertaken by Canada in this area. As you know, Mr. Speaker, in addition to the oil and gas resources of these areas, there are also other resources, such as our fisheries, which are a very important source of revenue for Canada. Minerals are also part of the resources which could be available to Canada. In the years to come, in the nineties and in the next century, when plankton and other marine resources may become marketable, this coastal zone will be an extraordinary asset for all Canadians. We have just started to develop these resources, and already the provinces are arguing to know to whom they belong. Ownership of the natural resources in these lands is still not recognized internationally, and the provinces, which can do nothing in international law in this regard, have already started to criticize and speak about sharing.
I feel that the offers made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to Newfoundland during the last election show his broad outlook on the matter of sharing the revenues from those resources. And I further submit that the matter of knowing who owns the resources is one thing and who is going to benefit from those resources is quite another. Mr. Speaker, as a Canadian and a Quebecer, I own in Quebec part of the offshore resources and I am ready to share them with my fellow-Canadians. However, I am amazed that my opposition colleagues, especially those from the western provinces, excluding British Columbia, oppose such a measure. Because barring any unforeseeable geographical disaster, I find it hard to visualize how Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario can start speculating on the resources outside the 200-mile limit, because those provinces have no coast.
In the year 2000, I believe that the resources we have offshore which are shared by many provinces, except the western provinces, of course, not including B.C., will probably be exploited on a larger scale than today, and more than petroleum and gas will be exploited in these regions. I just question the purpose of an hon. member from Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba saying, only today, that we do not want to include this in the legislation when actually, in the year 2000, they will share the resources and the revenue of

July 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
these properties. I just question the motive and 1 think that it is probably in support of today's problems.
However, I feel that we can have a long-term policy. We should think of Canada on a long-term basis. When we think about sharing today and tomorrow and about the existence of this country, we must remember that Canada can extend its shores to the 200-mile limit. We should keep this provision in Bill C-48 and think about the future, not be shortsighted and just think about tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, if reference is made to the known offshore resources, some information should be shared. Panarctic Oil, 45 per cent owned by the Canadian government, has been doing a lot of work, and in 1979 the Canadian government spent more than $600 million on the development of oil and natural gas. Certain provinces probably can spend that kind of money, but I would be very surprised if most provinces could invest such huge amounts of money to develop the offshore energy potential. That is why I firmly oppose the Progressive Conservative Party's amendment.
And based on the notes for a speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) at the Financial Post Offshore Canada Conference held in Halifax on June 23, 1981, I would like to repeat some basic facts emphasized by a minister coming from a coastal area. And I quote:
The encouraging prospects found off the Atlantic coast could make a very significant contribution to this country's energy picture. A total of some 5 trillion cubic feet of gas and 1 billion barrels of oil have already been discovered off the Atlantic coast. According to federal geologists, that area could contain from 7.5 to 12.5 billion barrels of oil and between 70 and 125 trillion cubic feet of gas. That is nearly 20 per cent of all known and expected oil and gas resources in Canada, and nearly half the amount of oil and gas already discovered in the western provinces.
At this point, Mr. Speaker some 150 wells have been drilled off the Atlantic coast. In all, some $900 million have been spent since the beginning of drilling operations. But despite all those efforts, we still do not have one single producing oil well in that area. Research is being conducted and rigs are being set up and, hopefully, we will benefit from these resources in the not too distant future. According to the National Energy Program, we will spend yet another $200 million in 1981 and some $400 million in 1982. Such financial commitments will enable the Atlantic region to develop offshore Canada lands. However, if we look at what has happened in European countries, specifically in the North Sea, we realize that enormous investments must be made before this potential can be tapped.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, instead of taking a very narrow view, instead of fighting over the distribution of revenues even before starting to develop these natural resources which have not even been ruled Canadian property, since, as I just mentioned, the 200-mile zone has not yet been recognized in international law as Canadian land per se, and it will not be in the international perspective, international treaties, if ratified, will decree that natural resources can be the property of the
coastal territory but that the land as such, the submarine lands, will not belong definitively to the coast entity.
It seems to me that we are splitting hairs. At this time, in the light of the extremely positive steps taken by the Canadian government in the last 20 years for the benefit of all Canadians in extending its territory, and especially with regard to the development of offshore resources, in the light of the dynamic role played by Canada at the 1975 Environment Conference where Canada actually started to get other countries to ratify the extension of coastal areas, we should rejoice instead of cry over our fate at the thought that offshore resources in the Atlantic will belong to strangers when those strangers are in fact other Canadians.
I think we should be able to discuss sharing those resources and their benefits in harmony. We should approach the subject in a positive frame of mind. I am sure the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) spared no effort in trying to find solutions acceptable to all Canadians. As a Quebecer, Mr. Speaker, I plead with this assembly to show some generosity in the sharing of those resources which all humanity can envy us. Mr. Speaker, I know of no other country with as small a population as ours and as great an energy potential that can at times be so narrow-minded about it. Our future depends on it, Mr. Speaker. I feel the notion of "Canada lands" must not be a narrow one but a generous one; and that is why I urge my hon. colleagues to vote against the amendment of the Progressive Conservative Party.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may begin my remarks by making a comment on those which we have just heard from the hon. member for Mercier (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette), there is no one in this House who is opposed to sharing the resources of Canada with Canadians. No one!

I am not going to take anything from anyone who says, "As a Quebecer, I am prepared to share what I have with Canadians." Everyone in this House is prepared to share. What is preventing the sharing of the resources of this country is the conflict of jurisdiction, the conflict of ownership and the conflict of property.
At the present time we are a retarded nation because the federal government refuses to acknowledge the rules laid down in our constitutional documents that accorded the resources to the provinces in 1930. Now we are talking about sharing as though there is a niggardly attitude; there is no niggardly attitude in this country about sharing.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: There never has been.

speechtext:
And there never has been. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that yesterday the debate on the
July 15, 1981

amendment was punctuated by a number of points of order or appeals to relevancy from the other side whenever a speaker on this side raised the question of revenue or money in the general discussion on the amendment proposed in motion No. 3.
It is my contention and the contention of all members on this side of the House, I think, that the whole purpose of stretching the definition of Canada lands in legislation beyond that which is normally accepted, namely, north of 60, is to lay claim not just to land but to potential revenue-producing land.
I suggest that we might call Bill C-48 and particularly the section on definitions in a Clause 2 a matter of maritime gerrymandering. The government is trying to secure, by legislation, what it is unable to secure by negotiation. It is as simple as that.
Revenue and the Canada lands concept are intimately linked in this debate, Mr. Speaker. We cannot avoid that. The Liberals are talking Canada lands and they want us to stay with Canada lands, but what they mean is revenue from Canada lands. We are merely exposing this double talk. If there is any doubt, I suggest that hon. members look at Clause 9 and Clause 40 of the bill for the definition of Canada lands.
Clause 9 defines the method of licensing and exploration agreements, while Clause 40 deals with royalties from Canada lands.
It is all very well to say that we have to stay with the lands deal, but I insist that we must think in terms of the revenue that those lands are likely to produce. There is no question in my mind nor in the minds of a good many Canadians that the government in short of revenue and wants more. The argument for claiming the legislative right to more, through this bill, is that it is bankrupt. It is out of money. It is insolvent.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
I will tell the hon. member why. It is because of its disposition to squander the resources that are available to it. Its cash flow is non-existent. Indeed, it is flowing backwards, it is not only taxing for revenue but it has to borrow from taxpayers to increase its revenue and to pay the interest on the indebtedness.
In this connection I suggest that all hon. members and everyone who is listening should refer to page 11176 of Hansard for July 3, where there is a table showing the standing of the national debt from the time of confederation until today. I note the date, July 3, and I note that this is a strange way to commemorate members of the House coming together after the Dominion Day break.
In 1867, the national debt was $76 million net; in 1941, in the middle of a war, the net public debt was $4 billion; in 1968, the year the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his governing team took office, the debt was $16.7 billion, or four times greater than it was in the middle of the war. Today the debt has increased four and a half times to $82.7 billion net.
We can see why the government is out in the maritimes, gerrymandering. It is on the grab. We should not be surprised that it is looking for new sources of revenue, and hence is
Canada Oil and Gas Act
seeking to broaden the definition of Canada lands and the royalties that can be obtained from the resources that those lands will provide.
If the government wants to show its good will, I suggest that it withdraw the notice of appeal it has lodged against an opinion of the B.C. Supreme Court which assigned to the provinces, by a decision of three to two, the waters between the mainland of British Columbia and the large offshore island and the chain of the Charlottes. The B.C. Supreme Court ruled that those waters belonged to the province and immediately the federal government lodged an appeal to contest the ruling.
I should like to go into this carefully because I think it is very important. It has been referred to by other hon. members so I will confine my remarks almost exclusively to one aspect of the matter.
For the definition of Canada lands I would refer hon. members to clause 2 of the bill, which reads, in part, as follows:
"Canada lands" means lands that belong to Her Majesty in right of Canada, or in respect of which Her Majesty in right of Canada has the right to dispose of or exploit the natural resources and that are situated in
(b) those submarine areas, not within a province,-
"Not within a province" is what we seek to have removed, Mr. Speaker. If the government wants to demonstrate its good intentions, it should look at this clause in light of the B.C. Supreme Court ruling and its intention to appeal that judgment.
The B.C. government sought an opinion on a question regarding its property rights on land covered by the waters of the Strait of Juan de Fuca, the Strait of Georgia, the Johnstone Strait and the Queen Charlotte Strait. The court ruled three in favour and two against the lands being the property of the Queen in right of the province of British Columbia.
This question of discontinuity as between the mainland and the islands must underlie the decision of the federal government to appeal that ruling. No sooner had this particular ruling come down than the federal government decided to appeal. I think on the basis of it, it is beyond imagination's wildest hallucinations to suggest that the land attaching offshore land to the mainland of a province is not part of a province. Yet two justices out of five ruled that way. The three ruled that those submarine lands did belong to the province of British Columbia.
What disturbs me and many British Columbians is that the central Liberal government has served notice of intention to appeal that ruling to a higher court, presumably the Supreme Court of Canada, where, incidentally, one of the dissenting judges now sits.
What the dissenting judges are arguing and what the federal government is now suggesting by maintaining its intention to appeal this ruling, which is not yet implemented, is that there

July 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
is such a phenomenon as a discontinuous province; that a province can be interrupted territorially or maritimely, if you like, in its seaward expansion, and that the interrupted portion could become a part of the central government. I suggest this is really not a very satisfactory way to run a federation. I would call it the doctrine of provincial discontinuity.
I suggest that if it were applied in its full intent it would probably apply in the mouth of the Gulf of St. Lawrence and to the waters of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, which would be interrupted by federal jurisdiction between the province of Quebec and Anticosti Island, and the federal government would claim the river bottom there.
I consider that doctrine of provincial discontinuity as one that is hardly tenable in any court of law. The only example I can think of at the moment, and that broke up, was the example of East and West Pakistan which were interrupted by another state, India. But to have east and west British Columbia interrupted by a section of territory or maritime area assigned to the central government is verging on the ludicrous, the ridiculous, if not the improbable. It is also verging on providing a very good cause for the breakaway of one province from Canada. I do not know whether they have ever thought of that. It would at least add another argument, if indeed a further argument is necessary, to persuade British Columbians that Ottawa has no sensitivity to their problems, and that B.C. and other western provinces might do better without Ottawa.
Therefore, as a mark of honourable intention, I suggest this to the parliamentary secretary, since he is the ranking guy here, I think, there being no ministers in the House. The central government ought to withdraw its notice of appeal against the ruling of the B.C. court. This would go a long way, I suggest, toward re-establishing an atmosphere of confidence and trust between the two levels of government, an atmosphere that has been sadly fogged for the last ten years or more.
It would seem that the doctrine of confrontation is that which governs the relations between this government and the provinces-a deplorable situation and I regret that it should be that way.
One might almost say that not just the waters at the mouth of the St. Lawrence, which is closer to the federal government, and therefore they can understand that-I do not think they understand what the waters between the islands and the mainland of British Columbia mean-might be declared in the same way the government is thinking of declaring as federal waters, but presumably the subsoil over which those waters flow would then become national territory. At least the government is testing that ruling of the B.C. Supreme Court. I suspect that would not go down very well with the province of Quebec. I suspect, in fact, that because the province of Quebec would be a party en cause, the claim would not even be made. But in British Columbia where the government has no member of the cabinet, and whose problems the government does not even understand, it is prepared to leave it stand as a threat to the province.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 first want to indicate my appreciation for the wide latitude you have permitted in this debate. In looking at the various amendments to this bill one recognizes that perhaps motion No. 3 is the only motion on which we could have a wide ranging debate on the entire bill, the entire energy policy and, indeed, a number of constitutional matters. 1 might say that having listened for several days to this debate the debate has ranged widely. I am sure you will allow me the same latitude in the course of the 20 minutes I have, in which I hope to have my say in this House on this bill.
The first thing I want to say about the bill is that it is very complicated and very crucial to Canada. We have had hearings on this bill in the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works for approximately six months, with approximately 73 meetings and 130 witnesses. I think it is appropriate that somebody put on record some of the groups which came before this committee because it does give an excellent indication of the importance of this bill. They included most of the major oil companies and their respective organizations, such as CPA and IPAC, They appeared before the committee and made submissions. Several chartered banks appeared before the committee and made submissions, as did the Canadian Bankers' Association. The Canadian Bar Association and the Eastern Fishermen's Federation appeared. The Canadian Ocean Industries Association, the Canadian Shipbuilding Association, the Canadian Labour Congress and the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union also appeared and made presentations.
A number of native organizations also appeared, including the Native Council of Canada, representatives of the Dene nation, the Council of Yukon Indians, the Metis Association of the Northwest Territories and the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada.
The government of the Northwest Territories, the government of the Yukon, the chamber of mines of the Northwest Territories and the chamber of mines of the Yukon appeared and made representations. Indeed, one of the most pleasant presentations was by the mayor of Inuvik.
July IS, 1981

The Vancouver Board of Trade appeared and made a presentation, and several environmental organizations including the West Coast Environmental Law Association and the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee appeared. Other organizations came before the committee to make their presentations on this very important piece of legislation. Some of us had the opportunity and, indeed, the good fortune to listen to almost all of these presentations, and those we did not hear we read. I count myself in that group of few people who were fortunate enough to have this opportunity.
I mention all these organizations because today I want to take this opportunity to thank these organizations and people who came before the committee to make their cases. I hope everyone in the House wishes to thank them and to congratulate them for taking the time to come and put forward their cases. They participated in the democratic process eminently well with respect to this bill.
All these organizations were responsible for a substantial number of changes to this bill. Indeed, the initial draft of this bill left much to be desired, and by the time these organizations were finished with the bill, the government felt it necessary to bring forward many amendments and changes to accord with their wishes. In many cases those changes weave or interweave with some of the suggestions of the opposition. As I indicated, the influences were substantial, and I suggest they will continue to be so because literally every one of these groups and organizations will watch the passage and implementation of this bill very keenly, with great anticipation in some instances and with much regret in others.
I must say that I was disappointed that none of the provinces took time out to appear and make presentations to the committee on this very important bill which affects so many provinces. As I indicated before, this bill will have a profound effect on governments in Canada and on the opening up of what is two-thirds of this nation, the northern part.
If there is anything I would wish to say, I would publicly commend the chairman of the committee, who I think handled himself very well and gave every advantage to the groups which appeared so they could put their cases forward. I refer to the hon. member for Chateauguay (Mr. Watson).
There was a number of very important concerns, and they might be identified in about ten or eleven categories. The first was the definition of Canada lands. This amendment would effectively reduce Canada lands by approximately 50 per cent and would exclude from this bill Hibernia, the Beaufort Sea and most of the PanArctic gas discoveries in the north.
The second thing about which we were really concerned was ministerial discretion. This bill allows an enormous amount of ministerial discretion. We wish it had given the minister additional discretion in some other areas and removed it in many of the areas in which the minister is allowed wide ranging discretion.
Third, we were vitally concerned about the retroactive expropriation feature which was initially in this bill. Fortunately, because of the massive revulsion of the industry and
Canada Oil and Gas Act
some of the groups involved, the government felt it appropriate to back off the policy position it had imposed in the bill. The very unfortunate and almost despicable policy position regarding retroactive expropriation of rights and properties should under no circumstances be supported by any party in this House. Due compensation and access to due process of law should always be a right of Canadians in this democratic country.
Some hon. Miembers: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Much concern was expressed about the Crown-carried interest and the extent of the proposed nationalization of the oil industry on Canada lands. Some excellent arguments were made in this regard. There was great concern expressed about native peoples and, indeed, about the use of Canadian manpower and Canadian materials. There was a great deal of concern expressed about the effect of energy development and growth in the north on territorial governments and the municipal governments of some of the smaller settlements in the north. Some of us felt very strongly that some of the royalties accumulating from oil and gas production in this vast area should be placed in a fund for the future use of the provinces and for the future use of some of the communities which will have to develop under adverse conditions-and rather explosively because of this bill.
Environmental matters were a great concern, and we do not think the bill deals adequately with the concerns which will evolve in this area. There were many punitive measures which had to be adjusted, but one of the most important single aspects of this bill was the nature of its construction in terms of limiting the opportunities of small Canadian companies and their ability to participate in the development of oil and gas in this vast area of Canada, which is literally two-thirds of the country. This was one of my most basic concerns. Here was a bill to Canadianize an industry, and the restrictions, monetary and otherwise, on small Canadian companies participating were overwhelming in some areas.
Our country is vastly endowed with hydrocarbon resources, including coal, oil, gas, oil sands and heavy oils, as no other country in the world, but what we are suffering from is the lack of a proper management program and, particularly over the last decade, political mismanagement of the development of our hydrocarbon resources.
Bill C-48, in tandem with the National Energy Program, is an attempt to bring forward a new energy supply, distribution and use regime. First let me state unequivocally that the regime, although having some good aspects, is being forced upon a nation over too short a time-frame. That is one of the reasons there is a major revulsion in the United States against the regime. It is too fierce and too fast to accomplish objectives which may be appropriate over a longer time-frame.
What are the objectives? The objectives have been well stated on a number of occasions. The first objective is at least 50 per cent Canadian ownership of oil and gas production by 1990 through the process of Canadianization and nationalization. The second objective is Canadian control of a significant

July 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
number of large oil and gas firms. We know the manner in which the government is proceeding in this regard.
Third is an increase in the share of the oil and gas sector owned by the Government of Canada. I might put that in a different way: I might say a significant transfer of control over the oil and gas industry from the producing provinces, particularly Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, to federal control. The question is: How is it being done? Well, in three ways. First of all, by transferring the emphasis to Canada lands and away from provincial lands by taxation, rent and incentives. Secondly, by massively increasing the federal take from oil and gas produced in provincial land. We have seen only a beginning in that direction. Third, by the imposition of a federal oil and gas pricing regime which limits provincial government and company revenues from oil and gas produced from provincial lands.
From all the questioning we have done, we anticipate a two-price policy, a world price for oil produced in Canada lands. Petro-Canada has stated that unequivocally in committee. Under questioning the minister gave us every indication that oil from federal lands would be priced at world levels. Contrast this with a pricing structure for oil from provincial lands which is now approximately 50 per cent of the world price. So what we are attempting here is a transfer of control over the industry, putting emphasis on development of federal lands, not only through the tax and grant structure but through a price structure, and thereby depressing development in the provinces. I also want to touch on the Cold Lake project in relation to the policies associated with Bill C-48 and the NEP.
There is no doubt that there are very good arguments for moving in this direction if you have certain policies in mind and a certain vision of the nation. Canada's resources are what make this nation rich and make every one of us unique. We have in this nation elbow room, wealth, ability, capability and possibilities down into the future that no other nation in the world has. Heaven help us if we start to split it up because we will all suffer drastically.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am concerned about this amendment in regard to the vast seas of the northern part of Canada. It is my view and my conclusion that we must exercise sovereignty over that part of our nation in every possible way and at every instant. We must be there constantly because that vast area of Canada is looked upon with great envy by some of the major powers of the world. So if you ask me about my view with regard to that vast northern area, we must declare repeatedly that it is Canadian, and we must be there to exploit, develop, control and manage its resources.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Now, I want to touch briefly on the rights of the Atlantic provinces with regard to the resources extending for 200 miles out on the continental shelf. I am of the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that laws and court cases will not settle the question.
The provinces do not want to go to court or they would have been there a long time ago. It is negotiations which will settle this problem. My fear and concern is in connection with the negotiating process established during the last year by the government, which I find badly wanting.
I am terribly sorry that I will not have more time to dwell on this matter. What I want to say above all else is that any federal cabinet dealing constantly with the provinces must have somebody to take strongly the provincial point of view. The rest of the cabinet ministers are going to be building empires, taking the federal perspective, so there must be someone in cabinet who understands the provincial perspective and who will try and sell cabinet members and the caucus on the provincial perspective. There must be a minister of federal-provincial relations whose sole reason for being is to understand provincial aspirations, needs and desires, one who constantly projects them into cabinet over and over again. I for one am terribly disappointed that this government does not have a minister of federal-provincial relations who will totally carry the ball for the provinces on the Atlantic coast and the west coast on resources, cost-sharing programs and so forth. I suggest this government had better seriously rethink the need for appointing such a minister.
The then minister of intergovernmental affairs in 1978, the now Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde)-and he was a fairly effective minister of intergovernmental affairs in those days-gave a remarkable speech at the first ministers' conference where he said: "A century ago Sir John A. simply announced what his national policy was going to be. No discussions with provincial governments, no series of visits to provincial capitals, and no federal-provincial conferences preceded his announcements, and no one seems to have expected that they would. By contrast, any policies and processes we decide upon in this area today will emerge as a result of the process of federal and provincial consultation begun in the months preceding this meeting, and as a result of the continuing process of consultation which I hope the first ministers will agree to today."
His dissertation at that meeting was entitled "Consultative Mechanisms". That is what we need more of. That is what we need to bring unity to this nation, to bring the outer regions into the centre, and we need it quite soon.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to enter the debate on this motion during report stage on Bill C-48, a bill which we all know is to regulate oil and gas interests in the Canada lands, and to amend the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act.
I represent, as most members know, what could be termed an energy disadvantaged region of the country. Regardless of what happens in the future in energy exploration off the east coast, the most South West Nova can probably expect, as indeed most of the region, are some spin-off benefits from development taking place in a few growth centres. Mind you, I will be working hard for South West Nova to obtain these spin-offs.
July 15, 1981

Much of the debate on this motion has been concerned with jurisdiction and with what should constitute the Canada lands to which the act will apply. This is not surprising in view of the amount of political mileage opponents of the program are receiving from the jurisdictional question. In my view, the jurisdictional controversy is a red herring which may obscure the fact that the greater issue is the development of offshore resources.
The question of what is or what is not Canada lands is sidestepping the real issue. The real issue is this: Do we want control over our energy supply, distribution and pricing, and decisions about development of new sources-in effect our entire energy future-to reside with those who have a vested interest in meeting the needs of Canadians or with the vagaries of an increasingly anarchic free market? Those who insist upon drawing fine lines over jurisdiction of frontier areas are either playing fast and loose with our collective future for shortterm political gain, or attempting to sidestep the crucial question of whether control of Canada's future energy supplies, will reside in the hands of Canadians or of foreign multinationals.
It is easy to make references to "just birthright", as I believe one Nova Scotia cabinet minister has done, when referring to ownership of offshore resources. It is not so easy to explain how the astounding costs of developing those resources will be met. It is not hard to see that without federal involvement in the development process provincial governments, assuming they had such control, would be forced to turn to foreign capital, which naturally entails foreign control.
For an illustration of this we have only to look at the Nova Scotia government's overtures to American business for capital to finance a tidal power development on the Bay of Fundy.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Where are we borrowing from?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
The hon. member wants to know from where we are borrowing. It is a prime example in Nova Scotia. While Premier Buchanan could have proceeded through the Maritime Energy Corporation and federal funding, which would have ensured that the development would remain under Canadian control and benefit Canadians as well as Nova Scotians, he elected to abandon the Maritime Energy Corporation and invited American interests to participate in the funding of the project.
This is fine, except that if it is ever built with United States funds instead of Canadian funds most of the power generated by the plant will be exported to the United States. With offshore energy development one can only expect the level of foreign control to be even greater. The federal policy is to ensure that the energy resources of Canada are developed for Canadians. There has never been any suggestion that the areas where these resources are located are to be deprived of any of the benefits of their development.
"Canada lands" clearly defines for those who are investing millions of dollars in offshore resource development where the federal regulations in Bill C-48 will apply. It is a clear
Canada Oil and Gas Act
statement of what the responsibility of the federal government to Canadians will be in the development of oil and gas on these lands. The jurisdictional problem is another issue. If the provinces feel they have a right to offshore resources, let them go to the courts; but in the meantime the development of offshore oil and gas should not be hindered by uncertainty. Canadians and east coast Canadians need a strong National Energy Program if we are to continue our growth as a country.
I might add that there is strong support for the federal government having jurisdiction over the offshore. I will not become involved in a debate which should take place before the courts, but even Sable Island about which we have heard a lot during the debate on this motion is under Section 91 of the British North America Act a federal responsibility. We could look at federal states such as Australia and the United States. Who controls the offshore? Both of the countries I have just mentioned do, not the states next to the offshore.
The Supreme Court of Canada ruled in the British Columbia reference case on offshore that the territorial seabed was not within the boundaries of British Columbia. International law recognized the rights of coastal states. The Geneva convention on the continental shelf granted to coastal states sovereign rights to explore the continental shelf and to exploit its a natural resources. Canada has claimed rights to the 200-mile limit and they have been recognized. The ongoing United Nations Law of the Sea Conference reached a consensus on the coastal state's exclusive economic zone of 200 miles.
I believe we must rely on ourselves, on Canadians, on Nova Scotians, if we want control over this vital part of our present and future. Only by retaining control of our resources within our own country can we ensure that Canadians, both business people and ordinary citizens, are the first to benefit from resource development or, indeed, even that such development is carried on in appropriate ways to meet Canadian needs and aspirations.
If Newfoundland and Nova Scotia are right, if their claims to offshore resources are found to be legitimate, what then? Should the rest of Canada be expected to foot massive bills for exploration if that exploration may ultimately only benefit one or two provinces? Could those provinces develop their resources on their own, or would they be forced to resort to opening the door to exploitation by big foreign interests? Who would ultimately benefit from such development? It would not be Nova Scotians.
I wonder if anyone in the Nova Scotia government has taken the trouble to ask the people of that province how they feel about the question of offshore jurisdiction. Do the people of the Atlantic provinces really support the idea of provincial control of the offshore? I would note in that regard that more Liberals were elected in the 1980 election than in the previous one, and certainly the then prime minister, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), was giving away the offshore to try to win votes. Our insistence upon federal jurisdiction over the offshore is well-established in precedents and in international law.

July 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
I do not think that by claiming jurisdiction anyone in the region seriously believes that Ottawa is out to rob them of their birthright. I consider it imperative that the people of Canada, through the federal government, have some input in future energy resource development decisions. Only in this way can we be assured that those decisions will be made with some regard for the legitimate needs of the people.
In these increasingly energy-short days when we are forced to develop more expensive energy sources, I believe it is only through the participation of federal agencies such as Petro-Canada that energy alternatives will be explored at all. The enormously expensive tar sands projects, upon which we will some day depend for crude oil supplies, oil and gas exploration off the east coast, and even Premier Buchanan's prize Annapolis Valley power demonstration project, were developed with the aid of federal money and without that federal money would in all likelihood not have come about when they did.
What is the alternative if we defeat this motion? Canada lands is the alternative. What do the provinces have? They must enter into arrangements with the federal government, and what is wrong with that?
Let us look at what the arrangements have been in the past. In February, 1977 Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island agreed to set aside their differences. They signed a memorandum of agreement for joint administration which would provide for a general revenue sharing arrangement of 75 per cent for the provinces and 25 per cent for the federal government. It was this memorandum of agreement which was later repudiated through changes in governments. As late as September 19, 1980, during the constitutional conference, the federal government offered an administrative agreement to the maritime provinces which would allow the 100 per cent of the revenues from the sales of fuel, natural gas and other minerals until those provinces reached a have position.
We should all take one minute to reconsider what Canada means. It has always meant the sharing of the wealth of Canada between the haves and the have-nots. Why would all of the Atlantic provinces not wish to share if they ever reach a point where they can? It looks as if that will be some time soon, with all the oil and gas which exists there. Why should they not wish to share their bounty with the rest of Canadians? The energies of the provinces, in my view, should be directed to arriving at arrangements with the federal government which truly benefit their areas. When they are negotiating these arrangements they would do well to put aside some of their political considerations and think about the people of all those provinces.
In conclusion, I do not believe that business alone, driven solely by the profit motive, can provide the assurance we need to approach the future with confidence. The National Energy Program has been criticized sharply by big business interests. I suggest those voices are speaking out of self-interest. We might do well to accord them less than total credibility.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the few remaining minutes this evening I too wish to touch upon the question of jurisdiction. It surprises me that the hon. member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) would repeat speeches written by the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan), the former Premier of Nova Scotia, written some ten or 15 years ago.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I would like to inform the House that I do my own research on my speeches. Maybe I do not have the opportunity to speak as often as the hon. member for Halifax-Dartmouth East (Mr. Forrestall), but I am sure that when he finishes his speech we will have to judge whose content is best.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
The hon. lady might do herself and our province some justice if she would do a little original research and stop reading old speeches.
Our claim is simple. We want what was ours before confederation, which has been ours by recognition and which this government is now trying to take away from us. There is no political argument which can be put forward to controvert the position of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. Not only is there no political argument which can be put forward but there is no legal argument either.
The Supreme Court of the province of British Columbia made it very clear in its decision that, the facts in that case were based on historical evidence which may be not only different but which, in fact, were recognized by the court as being significantly different as between the west coast and the east coast. There is no question about the historical facts or the legal facts. The only question is whether or not there is a will in this Parliament to extend to the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland the same entitlements which were given in 1912, for example, to the great provinces of Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba.
At that time, by the stroke of a pen and by the will of Parliament, without constitutional amendment, some 600,000 square miles-20 or 30 times the size of the province of Nova Scotia-was given away. I was about to suggest that it was an oversight; but the question did come up at the time as to whether or not there would be compensatory arrangements with other smaller, original parts of confederation. There was no great pressure in those days to redress that inequity. There was no great pressure from Atlantic Canada. But because there was not, you cannot today interpret that to mean that the right does not continue to exist-it does. It is a historical right. There can be no real serious question about the legality of it.
It has been suggested that the issue should be taken to the courts. The Premier of Nova Scotia once removed tried to use those arguments. I wish hon. members could have been in the legislature of the province of Nova Scotia when Senator Isaac Smith from the other place, in another capacity, dealt with the spurious notes which were coming down from Ottawa with respect to jurisdiction.
Everyone knows we will share. We are not concerned about the money; we are concerned about the propriety of ownership
July 15, 1981

and the right of entitlement. There has never been the question raised on this side of the House about the need for comprehensive, tight controls-none whatsoever. The province of Nova Scotia will give up to a central, singular authority environmental concerns, licensing concerns and all of the regimes which are important to develop the energy and resources which are there. The province will give those up for the sake of orderly development.
But you must always remember, Mr. Speaker, that, in fact, control is ownership. The Premier of the province of Newfoundland must have the right, since he is the one first associated, to influence. That right is impeded through ownership and the rate at which the resources off that coast are developed. He is the one who must have the right. He is the one responsible first to his people and for his people for the orderly development of the potential of the east coast. The same is true in the province of New Brunswick and it is certainly true in the province of Nova Scotia. About that there can be little historical or political doubt.
What we are asking for those people who have faith in Canada and Canadians-something which we see very seldom from members opposite-is that that simple request be recognized. Control must be centralized but ownership must not be in question. What this bill does by the stroke of a pen is take away from Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Newfoundland lands and resources which, under the British North America Act, they are entitled to. They are entitled to those lands in law. They are entitled to them by history. In fact, they are entitled to them politically.
SO)
The spuriousness of the argument put forward, and the fact that the hon. member for South West Nova would not recognize the simple difference between the words "control" and "ownership" rather shocks me. After all, she is a trained lawyer. She should understand that control can pass from time to time wilfully, and ownership can, as well; but ownership determines control.
If we give up ownership now we will have lost these lands and their potential resources forever. It was the eastern provinces which financed the development of the central part of this country. It was our fish, our timber and our offshore trading that set up the industrial heartland of this country. We did that without complaint for 150 years. Now the government wants to take away from us a reward, a due recognition? If what it wants to do is control it for orderly development, so that we can get at the resources and satisfy the investment, so we can control environmental concerns, by all means, let us have some common authority to deal with these questions. However, that does not, should not and must never compromise the question of ownership, and ownership is what we are talking about. Call it jurisdiction, if one wants. One may call it control if one wants. But is is simply ownership.
We got nothing at all in 1812. Our money was pouring into central Canada to develop the rich resources in the areas which were annexed by agreement. It was our money. Look at
Canada Oil and Gas Act
James Bay. Are we going to nationalize that? Is that going to become a Canada land? Not on your life!
Does Your Honour know what we have now? This is just one example. The gas and oil from the east coast will more than supply our needs beyond our lifetimes and our grandchildren's lifetimes. The development of it and the control that is wanted by this government is to force the development of a petrochemical industrial base in this country to locate where perhaps natural forces would not place it. We are going to remove from the source of gas and oil, a thousand miles inland, a petrochemical base. We in Atlantic Canada will be watchers of pipeline. Well, I say to the devil with you! The government is not going to get away with it!

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: The government will not build a unified country. That is its intention. The government does not care about the cost. It allows $500 million or $600 million to be invested in the development of a petrochemical industry in eastern Canada, but it does so in such a way that not one nickle will accrue to the benefit of Newfoundland or Nova Scotia, not to mention New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. We are objecting to this. This is what control is about: recognition of our ownership. Then we would negotiate the best place for the development of that petrochemical industry. However, if we do not have ownership, if ownership is vested in Ottawa, although I trust Canada, I do not trust the government.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: We will get it in the neck, and we will be watchers of pipeline. We will not be allowed to develop a resource base which will enable us to lift ourselves out of the economic morass and difficulties in which we have been. We all recognize that as Atlantic Canadians. Please recognize us as Canadians from other parts of the country.

speechtext: A massive money grab!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: It is a money grab. It is a resource grab. More than that, it is a serious deprivation of a historical right and a legal right. It is a political matter about which the people of Atlantic Canada have long believed there can be no question.

Mr. Speaker, I too am one of those who have sat through numerous meetings on the committee which debated this particular bill, and listened to over 100 different delegations, all of which had very serious concerns about many different aspects of this bill.
One of the main reasons 1 am pleased to be able to speak about the broad concept of Bill C-48 in this initial stage is that the bill proceeded through committee not in a very conventional way. We had a bill which contained roughly 86 or so clauses before a committee. The government introduced 115 amendments to its own bill. What we were really trying to do in that energy committee on Bill C-48 was not to debate the bill, to

July 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
improve it and to test it against its implementation out in the country; rather, what we were doing in committee was drafting a new bill. There were 86 clauses and 115 amendments by the government alone!
We had some amendments to the bill ourselves, and so did the members from the NDP. As I said, the reason I am pleased to be able to talk about this bill is that not one single amendment proposed by Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition or of the New Democratic Party was accepted by the members of the governing party in the committee. In fact, the parliamentary secretary who steered the bill through the House admitted to me-and that is when I walked out, toward the end of the deliberations-that the government had no intention of accepting any of the many amendments that we had made and that the other party had made.
So much for democracy! So much for the orderly process of what was once a proud institution on which Canadians could rely to test a matter which the government would lay before it against the will of the people. So here we are debating a bill with 86 clauses, which changes in a very fundamental way the very nature of our socioeconomic behaviour in this country, to which the government has introduced 115 amendments and stated publicly that it is in no mood or is in no way prepared to accept any amendments from the opposition.
1 said to my friends across the aisle at that point, as I walked out, that I had a lot of other things to do. I knew what
their amendments were. I knew that they had a bad bill. They knew it themselves or else they would not have brought in all these amendments. I do not know who their draftsmen were. Surely there must be people out there with the competence and capacity to state in legal language the government's intentions in this bill.
1 want to speak a little about the government's intentions, but I realize it is six o'clock. Therefore, I would like to call it six o'clock and take my opportunity to do that tomorrow.
